chapter_theme: After the usurper's fall his queen dies of the news, and Civakan spares his women with a choice of maintenance or gold; he takes the palace, has the wounded tended, sleeps through a night of grief and triumph, worships the Jina at dawn, and holds court among his kin, friends and allied kings.

cast.role: the hero, now victor over the usurper
Kattiyangaran's chief queen, who dies on hearing of his death (named only by the gold fillet in 2343)
the women of the dead usurper's household, whom Civakan spares
the palace women who bathe, attend and praise Civakan
Civakan's maternal uncle, king of Videham, who led the allied chariots
the allied kings who fought on Civakan's side
the merchant who raised Civakan, his foster father

2344.reading: Told that the bull-like usurper and his sons have fallen, his queen cries 'has it come to that?', sinks like a doe struck by a spear, her red eyes rolling up and sinking like carp in shallow water, and dies.
2344.nuance: The question in 2343 asks which of the women wore the gold fillet the usurper gave her; this verse follows on with her answer in death, so she is taken as his chief queen, though the verse never names her.
2344.event: Kattiyangaran's queen hears that he and his sons died in the battle, faints and dies.

2345.reading: Civakan tells the usurper's women that his fiery anger, hissing like the five-hooded snake, was let go when the cruel man breathed his last, and that they need not melt in fear like dark serpents caught in Garuda's beak.
2345.nuance: The anger is said to have been spent on the one enemy (வெய்யோன் உயிர்ப்பின் விடுத்தேன்): the victor draws a line between the usurper and his household.
2345.event: Civakan assures the dead usurper's women that his anger ended with the usurper.

2346.reading: He goes on: women of waists fine as a thread through a gem, of speech like song, he will do them no harm, and they should not let their long eyes rain tears like the red water-lily spilling pearls.
2346.event: Civakan promises the women he will not harm them and bids them stop weeping.

2347.reading: The broad-shouldered hero says they have nothing to fear from him: he will give them a living here to live on, or they may take gold and go and live elsewhere.
2347.nuance: The choice to stay or leave with gold is the epic's picture of a just conqueror's treatment of the fallen enemy's household; nothing is taken from them.
2347.event: Civakan offers the usurper's women maintenance in the city or gold to leave with.

2348.reading: Hearing the spear-bearer's words like the thunder of the sky, the women, whose small feet flinch from a red cushion as from fire, go off like a flock of young peahens to their own towns ringed with coconut and cane.
2348.event: The usurper's women leave the palace for their home towns.

2349.reading: Calling them a burden, they put off their ear-rings, sea-conch bangles, saffron and the weight of their flower garlands, roll pearl tears from their kuvalai eyes and sob, and grow pale like the ash of the champak.
2349.nuance: The putting off of ornaments is the mark of widowhood; the scene repeats, on the usurper's side, what Saccandan's women did at his death.
2349.event: The widowed women strip off their ornaments and weep.

2350.reading: When his soldiers, carrying bright lamps in their hands, have quickly searched every gold-walled hall and treasure chamber of the palace, he worships the goddess of the red lotus and goes in.
2350.nuance: The goddess of the lotus is Fortune (பூமகள், the ilampakam's name); entering the palace only after the search and her worship marks the taking of the kingdom.
2350.event: Civakan's soldiers search the palace, and he worships the lotus goddess and enters it.

2351.reading: Women of polished speech take watch over the scented flower bed made ready for the hero, with garlands of palm-like strands hanging down and fragrant smoke rising like mist from a hill.
2351.event: The palace women prepare and guard Civakan's bed.

2352.reading: He puts off his battle dress, is bathed by women with breasts painted in gold, and, his garland gleaming, bows to his uncle, lord of the host of chariots, and speaks.
2352.event: Civakan bathes, takes off his armour and bows to his uncle to speak.

2353.reading: He asks that the men whose chests the iron fouled in the battle have their wounds tended and be cared for, and then, while sweet-voiced women stroke his feet, the conqueror lies at rest like the lord on the serpent bed.
2353.event: Civakan charges his uncle with the care of the wounded and lies down to rest.

2354.reading: Elephants slashed by swords like hills full of wounds, the swift chariots, the horses unsaddled and the tuskers unharnessed, and the warriors with gaping spear wounds in their chests all breathe out in relief.
2354.event: The wounded army, its elephants and horses unharnessed, rests after the battle.

2355.reading: Amid the noise of deep wounds, the cries of weeping women scattering their ear-rings, the roll of drums, the conches, the flapping ears of elephants, the lutes and the songs of praise, the lord sleeps as if he heard none of it.
2355.nuance: The grief and the triumph of the night are heard together in one list, and the king's sleep is the still centre of it.
2355.event: Civakan sleeps through the night's noise of wounds, mourning and celebration.

2356.reading: While one group of bangled women swims in a sea of sorrow and another in a boundless sea of joy, the sun rises, and as women hold up fragrant garlands he washes his lotus eyes in clear water.
2356.nuance: Line 3's முப்பழநீர் is obscure, and which women grieve and which rejoice is left to the reader: the usurper's household against the victor's.
2356.event: At sunrise Civakan washes his face while some women grieve and others rejoice.

2357.reading: He bows his crowned head to the Lord, flings out red gold by the handful, has collyrium put on as the lamp of the triumphal adornment for a long life beyond thought, and takes up the bee-loud garland and his ornaments.
2357.nuance: முனைவன் is the Jina in this work's usage; worship and a gift come first in the morning order, before the king puts on his ornaments.
2357.event: Civakan worships the Jina, gives gold and puts on collyrium, garland and ornaments.

2358.reading: Praised by women, he puts on white silk kept in a gem casket, holds the five scents in his cheek, takes a kazhuneer flower in hand and sits like a lion on its couch, the noble one proud and a Kama even to the wise.
2358.event: Civakan dresses in white silk and sits in state.

2359.reading: The kings with flesh-smelling spears, who had seen the enemy's backs in battle, gather round the hero whose large hand, bright with bracelets, pours out wealth like a cloud.
2359.event: The victorious kings gather round Civakan.

2360.reading: His four kinds of old companions, his younger brother, his uncle, the hero's father, the rich city and the fertile country all gather quickly together in the palace.
2360.nuance: The father here (செல்வன் தாதை) can only be Kantukkatan, the foster father, since Saccandan is dead; the court that forms round the new king is his household of old, not the usurper's.
2360.event: Civakan's companions, brother, uncle, father, the city and the country assemble in the palace.

links.note: Vijayai, hearing the usurper's victory drum, fainted like a doe struck by a spear (எஃகு எறி பிணையின் மாழ்கி); the usurper's queen, hearing of his death, sinks like a doe that has taken a spear (வேலேறு பெற்ற பிணை ... மாழ்கி) and dies.
links.teaches: The epic gives the usurper's wife the very simile it gave the queen he widowed, so the wrong done at the start comes home in the same figure, except that Vijayai survived to bear the avenger and this woman does not survive.

links.note: Saccandan's women stripped off their necklaces, garlands and ear-rings and cried that the king's cruelty was cruel; now the usurper's women put off ear-rings, bangles and garlands as a burden.
links.teaches: The stripping of ornaments that opened the epic as the price of the usurper's deed closes his reign on his own women, showing that the widowhood he caused is the widowhood his household inherits.

links.note: After the first great battle Civakan made a gold image of the Jina, gave wealth and put away the sin of the battlefield with lament; after the final battle he bows to the Jina and flings out gold before putting on his royal ornaments.
links.teaches: Read with 820, the morning worship and gift of 2357 are not ornament but the same rite of expiation after killing, now made the first act of the new king's day.

links.note: After the earlier battle Padumukan tended the wounded with ghee and cloths and sent them to beds; here Civakan himself charges his uncle with the care of the wounded before he rests.
links.teaches: The care of the wounded moves from a friend's improvised kindness to a king's first order, so the epic marks Civakan's kingship by who is told to look after the men who bled for him.

links.note: The Nedunalvadai's king walks the camp at midnight, a few men with him, looking each wounded man kindly in the face; Civakan tells his uncle to have the wounded tended and lies down to rest with women stroking his feet.
links.teaches: Set beside the Sangam king who goes out in the cold to see the wounds himself, the epic's victor delegates the duty and sleeps, which shows how far the later court poem has moved the king's care from presence to command.

gains.a: an older measure of royal care for the wounded against which Civakan's delegation and rest stand out as a choice
gains.b: a contrast in which its king's personal midnight round reads as a distinct ideal, not the only way a poet could honour a king

links.note: The Mullaippattu's king cannot sleep for thinking of the elephant with its trunk cut, the men who fell and the wounded horses; Civakan sleeps through the noise of wounds, weeping women and drums as if he heard none of it.
links.teaches: The two kings face the same night after battle with opposite responses, the one kept awake by the wounded and the other asleep amid their cries, so the epic's sleep is a sign of a war ended where the Sangam king's waking is a sign of one still going on.

gains.a: a reason to read Civakan's undisturbed sleep as the peace of a finished war rather than mere indifference
gains.b: a view of its king's sleeplessness as tied to an unfinished campaign, which the poem alone does not test

links.note: Kalladanar asks whether the Pandya's spear did not stop short when he saw the widows of his enemies beating their breasts and cutting their hair; Civakan's anger stops at the usurper's death and he offers the widows a living in the city or gold to leave with.
links.teaches: Where the Sangam poem praises the conqueror only for holding back his spear at the sight of the widows, the epic makes restraint into provision, the victor feeding or endowing the women his war has widowed.

gains.a: an older warrior ethic of sparing the enemy's women, which shows Civakan's speech as the fulfilment of a known ideal
gains.b: an example of how far the restraint it praises could be carried, from not killing to giving the widows a livelihood

links.note: Purananuru 194 sets the dirge drum in one house beside the wedding drum in another and concludes that the maker of the world is unkind; in 2356 one band of women swims in a sea of sorrow and another in a sea of joy on the same morning, while the hero washes his face.
links.teaches: The epic puts the Puram poet's split world of grief and joy inside one palace and makes one man's victory its cause, so what the Sangam poet blames on the world's maker is shown here as the plain consequence of a deed.

gains.a: a reflective frame that names what is unsettling in its quiet line about two seas of feeling side by side
gains.b: a concrete case in which the division of grief and joy is made by a human act, not by an unkind creator

source_issues: 2354-2360 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2358 line 3 கமுநீர் is probably a misprint for கழுநீர் (as in 2346 line 3).
2351 line 1 (முலையீன்ற பெண்ணைத் திரடாமங்க டாழ்ந்து) and 2356 line 3 (முப்பழநீர்ப் பளிங்களைஇ) are hard to construe.
2357 lines 2-3, the collyrium as விளக்கு of the victory adornment, are obscure.
